items.title: The 'inert' gases are not entirely inert
items.claim: Argon, krypton, xenon and radon all form chemical compounds. XeF2, XeF4 and XeF6 are stable solids that can be bought from chemical suppliers. The textbook claim that noble gases 'don't react' is a simplification.
items.prompt: Why can xenon — but not helium or neon — form compounds?

options.text: Xenon has a different number of valence electrons

Xenon's outer electrons are far from the nucleus and weakly held (low ionisation energy, 1170 kJ/mol); the strongest oxidisers like PtF6 and F2 can strip or share them. Helium and neon hold their electrons too tightly
Xenon contains a hidden valence electron

items.reveal:
Until 1962, every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at the University of British Columbia noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) is essentially the same as xenon's (1170 kJ/mol). He had just shown PtF6 could oxidise O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.

XeF2 is now made by simply mixing Xe and F2 in sunlight. XeF4 forms colourless crystals. XeO3 is a powerful explosive. Krypton compounds (KrF2) exist at low temperature. Even argon was forced to form HArF in 2000.

Helium and neon, the lightest noble gases, have ionisation energies around 2080 and 2370 kJ/mol — too high to be broken even by the strongest oxidisers in normal conditions.
items.why: 'Inert' is a useful summary, not a law of nature. Strong enough chemistry breaks even the rule of full octets.

items.title: HF is a 'weak' acid that eats through glass
items.claim: Hydrofluoric acid has a pKa around 3.2 — classified as a WEAK acid. Yet it dissolves glass, etches silicon and is famously lethal.
items.prompt: Why is HF dangerous if it is a weak acid?

options.text: HF is actually a strong acid; the textbook is wrong
Acid strength (degree of ionisation in water) is separate from chemical reactivity — HF attacks Si-O bonds in glass and binds calcium in tissue, causing systemic toxicity unrelated to its pKa
HF reacts with skin's water to form a strong acid
HF only seems weak in dilute solution

items.reveal_title: Acid strength is not chemical reactivity
items.reveal:
HF's pKa around 3.2 means it only partially dissociates in water — strictly weaker than HCl, HBr, HI in that one chemical sense.

But HF's chemistry is dominated by fluoride. F- is a small, highly electronegative anion that forms exceptionally strong bonds to silicon (in glass) and beryllium and calcium. Glass etching: 4 HF + SiO2 to SiF4 + 2 H2O. HF poisoning: F- penetrates skin and chelates calcium and magnesium in blood and tissues, causing hypocalcaemia, cardiac arrest, deep necrosis.

A splash of 70 percent HF over 2 percent of body area can kill an adult.
items.why: Acidity (pKa) is the equilibrium constant for proton release in water. It tells you nothing about how reactive the conjugate base is or how toxic the molecule is.

items.title: Industry uses 'wrong' conditions for the Haber process
items.claim: The forward reaction N2 + 3H2 to 2NH3 is exothermic, and it reduces gas moles from 4 to 2. Le Chatelier says: high pressure, low temperature for maximum ammonia yield. Real plants run at 400 to 500 degrees Celsius — warm, not cold.
items.prompt: Why deliberately choose a temperature that lowers the equilibrium yield?

options.text: Cooling the reactor is impossible at industrial scale
The iron catalyst only works above 400 degrees
At room temperature the rate is so slow that even a high equilibrium yield is useless — moderate temperature is a compromise between rate (kinetics) and yield (thermodynamics)

items.reveal_title: Thermodynamics tells you what is possible; kinetics tells you whether it happens this century
items.reveal:
At 25 degrees Celsius the equilibrium for ammonia synthesis is excellent — but the activation energy is around 230 kJ per mol without a catalyst. The Maxwell-Boltzmann tail at room temperature has effectively zero molecules with that much energy. The reaction takes geological timescales.

The iron catalyst lowers the activation energy, and 450 degrees Celsius makes enough molecules energetic enough to react quickly. Yield drops to about 15 percent, but the unreacted gases are recycled. Throughput, not single-pass yield, is what matters.
items.why: Le Chatelier predicts the equilibrium destination. It says nothing about how fast you arrive.
